Reading · how friendships begin

1.1 Discuss. Think of a close friend. Do you remember your very first impression of them? Was it accurate?

KEY WORDS

an impression what you think of someone at first

to interrupt to speak while another person is speaking

evidence information that helps you judge

to survive to continue to exist after difficulty

The Friend I Almost Didn't Make

The first time I met Sevara, I decided within about four minutes that I didn't like her. We were sitting in the same university seminar, and she had already interrupted the tutor twice before I'd even taken my coat off. When she disagreed — loudly, and in front of everyone — with something I'd said about a book I hadn't actually finished reading, I remember thinking that the year ahead was going to feel very long.

For two months we avoided each other carefully. Then, one afternoon in November, I missed the last bus home. It had been raining since lunchtime, the library had closed, and I was standing outside the gates with a bag of borrowed books and no way of carrying them anywhere. Sevara walked past, stopped, looked at me for a moment, and said, without any warmth at all, “My brother's picking me up. Get in.”

We didn't say much in the car. But somewhere near the river she mentioned the name of the town where she had grown up, and I told her I knew it well; and by the time we reached my street we had worked out that our grandmothers had lived on the same road for twenty years. That was fourteen years ago. She was at my wedding. I was at hers.

I've thought about that evening a great deal since. What strikes me now is how certain I had been about a person I had known for four minutes. We usually make up our minds about people while we are still collecting the evidence, and then we quietly stop collecting it. Almost every friendship I value began badly, which makes me wonder how many others never got the chance to.

Grammar · narrative tenses

PRESENTATION

PAST SIMPLE — the main events of the story, in the order they happened:

I met her in September. We didn't speak for two months.

PAST CONTINUOUS — the longer background action around an event:

We were sitting in the seminar when she interrupted the tutor.

PAST PERFECT — something that happened before that past moment:

By the time we reached my street, we had discovered the connection.

Background / earlier action

Main event

I was waiting at the gates…

…when she walked past.

It had been raining all day, …

…so the ground was soaking wet.

She had interrupted twice…

…before I even sat down.

We were talking about a book…

…when she disagreed with me.

ERROR WARNING

Use the past perfect to show which action was earlier — not simply that it was long ago:

I had met her in 2010 and we had become friends. ✗ I met her in 2010 and we became friends. ✓

State verbs are not normally used in continuous forms:

I was knowing her before that. ✗ I had known her before that. ✓

Everyday English · telling a story and reacting

4.1 Read the conversation.

Nigora You'll never guess who I ran into yesterday.

Otabek Go on.

Nigora Kamila. We hadn't spoken since we fell out at university.

Otabek You're joking! So what happened?

Nigora Well, it all started when she apologised — before I'd even said hello.

Otabek Really? And what did you do?

Nigora In the end we sat in a café for three hours. We've made up.

Starting a story

Keeping it going

Reacting

You'll never guess what happened.

So then…

You're joking!

It all started when…

Anyway, …

Really? What happened next?

Well, the thing was…

In the end…

That's awful. / That's amazing.

ERROR WARNING

run into / bump into someone = to meet by chance:

I ran to an old friend yesterday. ✗ I ran into an old friend yesterday. ✓

Sequencing: at first · then · after that · in the end — NOT at the end when you mean finally.

Writing · a story

5.1 Write a story (120–150 words) about how you met someone important in your life. Use all three narrative tenses.

PLAN

Opening — set the scene with the past continuous: It was raining and I was waiting outside…

Middle — the main events in the past simple, with earlier information in the past perfect: I had never met her before…

Ending — how it finished and why it still matters: In the end… · Looking back, …

Useful phrases: It all started when… · At first… · After that… · Suddenly… · In the end…
